prompt: Polymers react like analogous small molecules. Which reaction does the section give for the aromatic rings of polystyrene?

choices.text: Typical electrophilic aromatic substitution
Radical-initiated halogenation
choices.why: The section gives that reaction for the alkane chains of polyethylene.

choices.text: Hydrolysis by aqueous base
choices.why: The section gives that reaction for the amide linkages of nylon.

choices.text: Ring-opening metathesis
choices.why: ROMP opens strained cycloalkenes (Section 31.5), not aromatic rings.

explanation: A polymer's chemistry is similar to that of analogous small molecules: the alkane chains of polyethylene undergo radical-initiated halogenation, the aromatic rings of polystyrene undergo typical electrophilic aromatic substitution, and the amide linkages of nylon are hydrolyzed by aqueous base.

prompt: Polymers experience much greater van der Waals forces than small molecules. In which kind of polymer are these forces strongest?

choices.text: One like high-density polyethylene, whose chains pack together closely in a regular way
One like poly(methyl methacrylate), whose chains can't pack together regularly
choices.why: Van der Waals forces act only at close distances, so poorly packed chains feel weaker forces. PMMA is noncrystalline.

choices.text: One with highly irregular, randomly coiled chains, like an elastomer
choices.why: Irregular chains can't pack closely, so van der Waals forces between them are weak.

choices.text: Any polymer heated above its melt transition temperature
choices.why: Above T_m the crystalline regions have melted to an amorphous material, so the chains are no longer packed closely.

explanation: Because van der Waals forces operate only at close distances, they are strongest in polymers like high-density polyethylene, in which chains can pack together closely in a regular way. The major difference between small and large molecules is in physical properties like these.

prompt: What are crystallites in a polymer?

choices.text: Highly ordered regions in which the zigzag chains are held together by van der Waals forces
Regions where chains are joined by many covalent cross-links
choices.why: Crystallites are held together by van der Waals forces, not covalent cross-links.

choices.text: Small crystals of plasticizer mixed into the polymer
choices.why: Plasticizers are small molecules that lubricate between chains. Crystallites are ordered regions of the polymer chains themselves.

choices.text: Regions where the chains are randomly coiled
choices.why: Random coiling is the opposite of crystallinity. Crystallites are highly ordered.

explanation: Many polymers have regions that are essentially crystalline. These crystallites consist of highly ordered portions in which the zigzag polymer chains are held together by van der Waals forces (Figure 31.7.1). Polymers with a high degree of crystallinity are generally hard and durable.

prompt: Why is linear polyethylene highly crystalline while poly(methyl methacrylate) is noncrystalline?

choices.text: The substituent groups on poly(methyl methacrylate) keep its chains from packing closely together in a regular way
Poly(methyl methacrylate) chains are much shorter
choices.why: The section attributes the difference to the steric requirements of substituents, not chain length.

choices.text: Polyethylene is highly cross-linked
choices.why: Linear polyethylene's crystallinity comes from regular, close packing, not from cross-links.

choices.text: Poly(methyl methacrylate) is soft at room temperature
choices.why: Poly(methyl methacrylate) (Plexiglas) is noncrystalline yet very hard at room temperature.

explanation: Polymer crystallinity is strongly affected by the steric requirements of substituent groups on the chains. Linear polyethylene is highly crystalline, but poly(methyl methacrylate) is noncrystalline because its chains can't pack closely together in a regular way.

prompt: What happens at the melt transition temperature, T_m, of a polymer?

choices.text: The crystalline regions melt to give an amorphous material
A hard amorphous polymer becomes soft and flexible
choices.why: That happens at the glass transition temperature, T_g.

choices.text: The polymer becomes highly cross-linked and sets into a hard mass
choices.why: That describes heating a thermosetting resin, not the melt transition.

choices.text: The chains break down into monomers
choices.why: Melting the crystallites changes physical order, not the covalent chains.

explanation: When a polymer with crystalline regions is heated, those regions melt at the melt transition temperature, T_m, to give an amorphous material.

prompt: What is the glass transition temperature, T_g?

choices.text: The temperature at which a hard amorphous polymer becomes soft and flexible
The temperature at which the crystalline regions of a polymer melt
choices.why: That is the melt transition temperature, T_m.

choices.text: The temperature at which a thermosetting resin cross-links
choices.why: Cross-linking on heating is what thermosetting resins do. T_g describes softening of an amorphous polymer.

choices.text: The temperature at which a polymer burns
choices.why: The section defines T_g as the point where a hard amorphous polymer turns soft and flexible.

explanation: Noncrystalline, amorphous polymers like poly(methyl methacrylate) can be very hard at room temperature. When heated, the hard amorphous polymer becomes soft and flexible at the glass transition temperature, T_g.

prompt: Into how many major categories does the section divide polymers by their physical behavior?
explanation: Polymers can be divided into four major categories by physical behavior: thermoplastics, fibers, elastomers, and thermosetting resins.

prompt: Which description fits a thermoplastic?

choices.text: A high glass transition temperature, hard at room temperature but soft and viscous when heated, with little or no cross-linking
A low glass transition temperature and a small amount of cross-linking, so it stretches and springs back
choices.why: That describes an elastomer.

choices.text: Highly cross-linked, solidifying into a hard, insoluble mass when heated
choices.why: That describes a thermosetting resin such as Bakelite.

choices.text: Extruded through a spinneret and drawn so its crystallites line up
choices.why: That describes a fiber.

explanation: Thermoplastics have a high glass transition temperature, so they are hard at room temperature but become soft and viscous when heated, and can be molded. Because they have little or no cross-linking, the individual chains can slip past one another in the melt.

prompt: Which pair contains one amorphous, noncrystalline thermoplastic and one partially crystalline thermoplastic, in that order?

choices.text: Polystyrene, then nylon
Polyethylene, then poly(methyl methacrylate)
choices.why: This is reversed. Polyethylene is partially crystalline, and poly(methyl methacrylate) is amorphous.

choices.text: Nylon, then polyethylene
choices.why: Both nylon and polyethylene are partially crystalline.

choices.text: Poly(methyl methacrylate), then polystyrene
choices.why: Both are amorphous and noncrystalline.

explanation: Some thermoplastics, such as poly(methyl methacrylate) and polystyrene, are amorphous and noncrystalline; others, such as polyethylene and nylon, are partially crystalline.

prompt: What is a plasticizer, and why is one added to poly(vinyl chloride)?

choices.text: A small organic molecule that acts as a lubricant between chains, making the brittle polymer supple and pliable
A cross-linking agent that makes the polymer harder
choices.why: Plasticizers do the opposite: they lubricate between chains so the polymer isn't brittle.

choices.text: A catalyst that raises the molecular weight of the polymer
choices.why: Plasticizers aren't catalysts. They are small molecules that sit between chains.

choices.text: A second monomer that forms a copolymer with vinyl chloride
choices.why: Plasticizers are added to the finished polymer and are not built into the chain.

explanation: Plasticizers are small organic molecules that act as lubricants between chains; they are added to thermoplastics to keep them from becoming brittle at room temperature. Poly(vinyl chloride) is brittle when pure but supple and pliable with a plasticizer, and is used for most hospital IV drip bags.

prompt: Dialkyl phthalates such as di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (dioctyl phthalate) are common plasticizers. What has the U.S. FDA advised about them?

choices.text: Using alternative materials in compromised patients and infants, while finding no evidence of toxicity for healthy individuals
Banning them from all medical devices
choices.why: The FDA advised alternatives for compromised patients and infants, not a total ban. Children's toys with phthalates are what have been banned in the United States.

choices.text: That they are toxic to all healthy adults
choices.why: The FDA found no evidence of toxicity for healthy individuals.

choices.text: That they are safe for all uses with no restrictions
choices.why: The FDA advised alternative materials for compromised patients and infants.

explanation: Questions have been raised about the safety of dialkyl phthalate plasticizers. The FDA has advised the use of alternative materials in compromised patients and infants but has found no evidence of toxicity for healthy individuals. Children's toys that contain phthalates have been banned in the United States.

prompt: Fibers are made by extruding a molten polymer through a spinneret, then cooling and drawing them out. What does the drawing do?

choices.text: It orients the crystallite regions along the fiber axis, adding considerable tensile strength
It melts the crystallites to make the fiber amorphous
choices.why: Drawing lines up the crystallites; it doesn't melt them.

choices.text: It adds cross-links that set the fiber into a rigid mass
choices.why: That describes a thermosetting resin. Drawing orients existing crystallites.

choices.text: It coils the chains randomly so the fiber can stretch and spring back
choices.why: Random coiling describes an elastomer. Drawing a fiber orients its crystallites.

explanation: Fibers are thin threads produced by extruding a molten polymer through small holes in a die, or spinneret. Cooling and drawing out the fibers orients the crystallite regions along the axis of the fiber and adds considerable tensile strength (Figure 31.7.2). Nylon, Dacron, and polyethylene have the semicrystalline structure needed to be drawn into fibers.

prompt: Which polymers does the section name as having the semicrystalline structure needed for being drawn into oriented fibers?

choices.text: Nylon, Dacron, and polyethylene
Poly(methyl methacrylate), polystyrene, and Bakelite
choices.why: PMMA and polystyrene are amorphous, and Bakelite is a thermosetting resin. None is the section's fiber example.

choices.text: Natural rubber, Bakelite, and nylon
choices.why: Natural rubber is an elastomer and Bakelite a thermosetting resin.

choices.text: Gutta-percha, natural rubber, and polystyrene
choices.why: These aren't the section's fiber examples; natural rubber is its example of an elastomer.

explanation: Nylon, Dacron, and polyethylene all have the semicrystalline structure necessary for being drawn into oriented fibers.

prompt: What must the chains of an elastomer be like?

choices.text: A low glass transition temperature, a small amount of cross-linking, and an irregular shape that prevents crystallites
A high glass transition temperature and no cross-linking
choices.why: That describes a thermoplastic, which is hard at room temperature.

choices.text: Extensive three-dimensional cross-linking
choices.why: That describes a thermosetting resin. An elastomer needs only a small amount of cross-linking.

choices.text: A regular shape that packs into many crystallites
choices.why: Crystallites would stop the chains from stretching and recoiling. Elastomer chains must be irregular.

explanation: Elastomers are amorphous polymers that can stretch and spring back. They must have low glass transition temperatures and a small amount of cross-linking to prevent the chains from slipping over one another, and the chains must have an irregular shape to prevent crystallite formation.

prompt: Why does a stretched elastomer return to its original shape when released?

choices.text: Van der Waals forces are too weak and too few to hold the straightened chains in their stretched orientation
Strong van der Waals forces between the straightened chains pull them back
choices.why: The section says the reverse: the forces are too weak and too few to keep the chains oriented, so they recoil.

choices.text: The chains form crystallites that snap back
choices.why: Elastomer chains must be irregular to prevent crystallites from forming.

choices.text: Covalent bonds break on stretching and re-form on release
choices.why: Stretching straightens and orients randomly coiled chains; it doesn't break covalent bonds.

explanation: When an elastomer is stretched, the randomly coiled chains straighten out and orient along the direction of pull. Van der Waals forces are too weak and too few to maintain this orientation, so the elastomer reverts to its random coiled state when the force is released (Figure 31.7.3).

prompt: Natural rubber is an elastomer, but gutta-percha is crystalline and nonelastic. What accounts for the difference?

choices.text: Natural rubber's cis double-bond geometry prevents close packing; gutta-percha's geometry allows the chains to pack better
Gutta-percha has no double bonds, while natural rubber does
choices.why: Both are chains with double bonds. The difference is the geometry of those double bonds.

choices.text: Natural rubber is highly cross-linked, while gutta-percha has no chains
choices.why: Natural rubber has only occasional cross-links, and gutta-percha is a chain polymer too.

choices.text: Natural rubber's double bonds let its chains pack into crystallites
choices.why: This is reversed. Rubber's cis geometry is irregular and prevents crystallites; that is why it is elastic.

explanation: Natural rubber has the long chains and occasional cross-links needed for elasticity, and its irregular cis double-bond geometry prevents close packing into crystallites. Gutta-percha's geometry allows better packing of chains, so it is highly crystalline and not an elastomer (Figure 31.7.4).

prompt: What is a thermosetting resin?

choices.text: A polymer that becomes highly cross-linked and solidifies into a hard, insoluble mass when heated
A polymer that becomes soft and viscous when heated so it can be molded
choices.why: That describes a thermoplastic.

choices.text: A polymer that stretches and springs back
choices.why: That describes an elastomer.

choices.text: A polymer whose crystallites are oriented by drawing
choices.why: That describes a fiber.

explanation: Thermosetting resins are polymers that become highly cross-linked and solidify into a hard, insoluble mass when heated. Bakelite, first produced in 1907, is the classic example.

prompt: How is Bakelite made, and what happens when it is heated?

choices.text: Phenol reacts with formaldehyde; on heating, water is eliminated and many three-dimensional cross-links form
Phenol reacts with formaldehyde; on heating, the chains slip past one another and the resin softens
choices.why: Softening on heating describes a thermoplastic. Bakelite sets into a rocklike mass when heated.

choices.text: Diphenyl carbonate reacts with bisphenol A; on heating, phenol is lost
choices.why: That makes the polycarbonate Lexan (Section 31.4).

choices.text: A diol reacts with a diisocyanate; on heating, CO2 is lost
choices.why: That describes polyurethane foam formation (Section 31.4).

explanation: Bakelite is a phenolic resin made from phenol and formaldehyde. On heating, water is eliminated, many cross-links form, and the polymer sets into a rocklike mass. The cross-linking is three-dimensional and so extensive that a piece of Bakelite is essentially one large molecule.

prompt: Bakelite has been in commercial use longer than any other synthetic polymer. In what year was it first produced?
explanation: Bakelite, a thermosetting resin first produced in 1907, has been in commercial use longer than any other synthetic polymer. It is used for molded parts, adhesives, coatings, and high-temperature applications such as missile nose cones.

prompt: Catalytic hydrogenation of natural rubber adds H2 to each C=C bond, giving repeating units of –CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH2–. Is the product syndiotactic, atactic, or isotactic?

choices.text: Atactic
Isotactic
choices.why: The answer to Exercise 31.7.1 labels the product atactic: the new chirality centers have no regular arrangement.

choices.text: Syndiotactic
choices.why: The methyl-bearing chirality centers don't alternate regularly. The answer to Exercise 31.7.1 labels the product atactic.

choices.text: None of these, because the product has no chirality centers
choices.why: Each CH(CH3) carbon is bonded to H, CH3, and two different chain segments, so it is a chirality center.

explanation: Hydrogenation of natural rubber turns each –CH2–C(CH3)=CH–CH2– unit into –CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH2–, creating a chirality center at each CH(CH3) carbon. The answer to Exercise 31.7.1 shows that the product is atactic.
